They were alike in many ways, Thomas Strong Gilbert Sr. and the son to whom he gave his name and who, prosecutors say, would eventually kill him.
Graduates of elite boarding schools and Princeton University, the two men were handsome, gifted athletes who — on the surface at least — seemed to be navigating the exclusive glide path of wealth, social position and success that has long defined life inside America’s upper crust.
All this exploded, however, when, the police said, Thomas S. Gilbert Jr., 30, marched into his parents’ apartment this month and
shot his father in the head
— after asking his mother to run out and get him a sandwich and a soda.
The attack shocked not only those who knew the Gilberts but also many more who live in their rarefied and intertwined world of hedge funds, private clubs and opulent homes in Manhattan and the Hamptons.
And the question was more or less the same: A good man had died, and no one knew why.
But in the asking of this question, a starkly different picture of the Gilbert father and son has emerged.
Among the many acquaintances of the two who were interviewed for this article, no one agreed to speak publicly given the legal and emotional sensitivities involved.
The senior Mr. Gilbert, who was 70, was a midlevel financier working punishing hours to get his small hedge fund off the ground. Gregarious and gentlemanly, he was a longtime member of the Maidstone Club in East Hampton and the River Club in Manhattan and, by all accounts, had a smile and a friendly word for everyone.
His son, on the other hand, had become a disturbed loner with few remaining friends, and had not held down a real job since graduating from Princeton in 2009. In the months before his father’s death, Tommy, as he was known to all, was under investigation related to a fire at a Hamptons house belonging to the family of his lifelong friend, and spent long hours at shooting ranges honing his skill with a pistol.
He was arrested just hours after fleeing his parents’ place on Beekman Place, a prestigious block on the far east side of Manhattan, to his own apartment on West 18th Street in Chelsea, where his father was paying the $2,400 monthly rent. A bag was packed, and the police confiscated credit card forgery equipment.
The Manhattan district attorney’s office has charged Mr. Gilbert with murder in the second degree, and he is at Rikers Island until Feb. 5, when the charges against him will be made public at a court hearing. He has not entered a plea.
Continue reading the main story
But for the moment, at least, the few facts related to the case offer scant explanation as to why Thomas Gilbert Jr. would have taken such a rash step.
A senior police investigator, who was unauthorized to speak publicly about the case, described the younger Mr. Gilbert as being upset with his father for cutting back on his allowance, said to be around $600 a week. One lawyer uninvolved in the case but who knew both the father and the son expressed doubt that this could be the sole motivation for the son to have committed such a crime, as he is charged.
“I can’t believe he would kill his father for a $100 reduction in allowance,” said the lawyer, who declined to identify himself because of the sensitivity of the subject.
This may well be true, but several acquaintances, and those who closely follow New York society, say that money — or the relative lack of it — in some way played a role in the son’s unraveling.
Michael M. Thomas, a former investment banker and a
novelist of Wall Street manners
, said that if he were ever to write a book about his own privileged upbringing, he would title it “Orphans With Parents.” Meaning that despite the private clubs, the best schools and all the many things that money can buy, there has always been for those born into this world a sense of acute loneliness that can strain ties with parents and mark a child forever.
Of course, in the case of the younger Mr. Gilbert, there was much more to it than that. According to people who knew him, he had numerous psychiatric maladies and for years had received various forms of counseling and medication.
Nevertheless, said Mr. Thomas, who did not know the family, even though Tommy was born into a culture that “disdained money,” he soon found himself in a world that, much more so than in his father’s time, had come to worship it.
“That can put you in a weird place,” Mr. Thomas said.
The Gilberts had money, of course. Mr. Gilbert, the father, had a weekend home in East Hampton’s exclusive Georgica Association enclave, and he was the sole owner of his newly established hedge fund, Wainscott Capital Partners, named after another Hamptons neighborhood.
Still, he was no magnate, as the size of his $1.6 million will attests. Beneficiaries include his wife; his 24-year-old daughter, Clare, an aspiring writer who has a
book-themed blog
; and his son. Whether Mr. Gilbert will be able to collect or not depends on the ultimate resolution of the criminal charges, lawyers say.
About a third of Mr. Gilbert’s estate comprised his hedge fund stake, with the remainder being other investments, property and cash.
Continue reading the main story
There had been some modest downsizing. Mr. Gilbert was in the process of selling his Georgica house. He and his wife had previously lived in a brownstone on the Upper East Side and were now renting a more modest apartment at 20 Beekman Place.
And while Mr. Gilbert’s hedge fund had grown last year to $7 million from under $2 million — with another $8 million expected in 2015 — it was still a relative minnow, much too small to spin off the lucrative profits that larger funds can produce.
At the same time, the younger Mr. Gilbert, who had long harbored his own dream of setting up a hedge fund (he had even given it a name: Mameluke Capital), found himself struggling to keep up with his well-pedigreed peers who had begun ascending the ranks of Wall Street and Manhattan society.
For him, life had always been something of a struggle, notwithstanding his top-notch education. He went to Buckley School in New York, then moved on to Deerfield Academy and then Princeton in 2003.
But it took Mr. Gilbert two extra years to graduate from college. And since 2009, his friends said, he led a fairly aimless life that involved surfing, yoga, many hours spent at the gym and parties.
There was an awkwardness to him, these people said. Women found him attractive, always impeccably dressed. He was a strapping 6 feet 3 inches, with thick blond hair that he often let grow, but those who knew him well said his unusual ways made long-term relationships difficult to sustain.
Continue reading the main story
His behavior was said to be erratic. He could be quiet and reserved, maybe even stutter a bit, but then explode in anger at a best friend over a woman, lash out at an attendant at the Maidstone Club or make an unwanted advance on a female friend.
As for the elder Mr. Gilbert, he could have leapt out of a
novel by Louis Auchincloss
, who chronicled in an earlier era the foibles of moneyed New Yorkers. These men worked hard, as lawyers and bankers, but it was their membership in the right clubs and their ability to marry well that allowed them to punch above their financial weight.
According to his
wedding announcement
in The New York Times, Mr. Gilbert’s father was the chief executive of a company that made machines for the textile industry. He was sent off to Andover and followed through with Princeton in 1966 and then Harvard Business School before starting a series of jobs on Wall Street.
But times on the Street were starting to change. It was no longer the case that having an entry in the New York Social Register — as Mr. Gilbert and his family did — would help you win a spot in a top investment firm.
Continue reading the main story
Mr. Gilbert had respectable jobs, for sure: for the longest period at Loeb Partners, a small investment bank, from 1984 to 1991.
But he also bounced around a bit, according to his
LinkedIn profile
. He founded an online educational company and was connected briefly to a biotechnology investment fund in 2010. A year later, he started Wainscott, which specialized in biotechnology stocks, with about $1 million of his own and other people’s capital, according to a person who had knowledge of his business dealings.
By contrast, Mr. Gilbert’s older brother, G. S. Beckwith Gilbert (Princeton ’63), became a successful leveraged buyout investor and prominent philanthropist who ran his own firm based in Greenwich, Conn.
Friends of Mr. Gilbert said that he had plans to build his hedge fund to a size of $1 billion, a heady goal for a man of that age. Still, he put in 12-hour days, worked the occasional weekend — when he was not playing golf, squash or tennis — and since the fund’s start, he had not taken a day’s vacation.
Over the last year, meanwhile, Tommy Gilbert was becoming increasingly violent, people who know him said.
In September, he was arrested in Southampton for violating a restraining order issued against him last summer after he beat up a childhood and family friend, Peter Smith Jr. He approached Mr. Smith at a beach party and asked him to reconcile, according to someone who was there. Mr. Gilbert flew into a rage after being rebuffed, friends said, and it was a short while later that the Smith family home in Sagaponack — a 350-year-old landmark — was burned near to the ground.
The Southampton police considered Mr. Gilbert a suspect, but a person with direct involvement in the case said that no charges against him were expected.
Suspect or not, after the fire, even his oldest pals began to keep their distance, and friends said that the younger Mr. Smith was convinced that his childhood friend wanted to kill him. Mr. Gilbert had begun to spend time at a shooting club on Long Island, friends said.
Family friends approached the elder Mr. Gilbert to express worry that his son was deteriorating. He was not welcome in his friends’ homes and was suspended from the Maidstone Club.
Those who did spend time with him in the last six months said that he had become very critical of his father, mocking his mannerisms, saying how he did not like the sound of his voice and complaining that he was too controlling.
Friends of the senior Mr. Gilbert say that his son rarely if ever showed up at the offices of his father’s hedge fund, even though the younger Mr. Gilbert wanted to set up his own fund.
Continue reading the main story
Continue reading the main story
Still, these people say, the father was well aware of his son’s troubles and had paid for the best medical and legal help possible. For example, about a year ago, Mr. Gilbert hired the high-profile lawyer Benjamin Brafman to help his son on what Mr. Brafman described as a “minor legal matter that was quickly resolved.”
Mr. Brafman said that his law firm handled Mr. Gilbert’s recent arraignment as a courtesy to the family. He said he was not certain if he would stay on to defend the younger Mr. Gilbert, and would not comment on any specific issues related to the shooting.
One friend recalled Mr. Gilbert coming over on Christmas and bringing cartons of Chinese food with him, even though he had been told that dinner would be served. He ate his food in silence and then left, the friend said.
It was a far different impression than the one he had left on friends and Maidstone Club members just two summers ago. At the time, he came across as gracious and well heeled, particularly on the tennis court, where he spent much of his time. “Tommy was a gentleman, and his father was a very nice man,” said one club member who played tennis with Mr. Gilbert and his father. “This is just such a sad story.”
Correction: January 16, 2015
An earlier version of this article misquoted the author Michael M. Thomas regarding his hypothetical book about his upbringing. Mr. Thomas said he would call his book “Orphans With Parents,” not “Orphans With Families.”

“
Virunga
,” one of 15 candidates shortlisted for the best documentary Oscar,  is a nature film with an edge.
The title refers to a national park in eastern Congo that is surrounded by armed rebel groups and besieged by poachers who have killed mountain gorillas, elephants and 140 of the rangers dedicated to protecting the park’s animals. That situation becomes even more toxic when a big British company begins to look for oil within the park’s boundaries.
Directed by Orlando von Einsiedel, “Virunga,” which counts Leonardo DiCaprio as an executive producer and has been
praised by Errol Morris
, focuses on the rangers and their struggle to keep the park running in one of the world’s poorest and most disorganized states. In particular, Rodrigue Katembo, a former child soldier turned biologist, and Andre Bauma, a quiet, dignified man who cares for orphaned gorillas with extraordinary tenderness and affection, emerge as heroic in their devotion to that cause.
Despite his  Teutonic name, Mr. von Einsiedel, 34, is British, born and raised in London. He studied social anthropology as an undergraduate, earned a master’s degree in development studies at the London School of Economics, and came to filmmaking through a very unusual route.
“I was a professional snowboarder for a number of years, from my teens into my early 20s, and I sort of learned the craft through making snowboard movies,” he said in an interview in New York last week. “In snowboarding you get sponsored and make money by wearing your sponsor’s clothing, but you also get extra money if you get in films or magazines. So there’s an incentive for you and your friends to learn to film each other.”
“Virunga” is Mr. von Einsiedel’s first feature-length documentary, though he has made several shorts, including “
Skateistan
,” about skateboarders in Afghanistan. During the interview, he talked about the challenges of telling a multilayered story in a war zone and working with animals. Edited excerpts follow:
Q.
The synopses of “Virunga” emphasizing the gorilla story line don’t quite do your movie justice. It is about a lot more than that.
A.
I never set out to make a movie about mountain gorillas. I always want to make films about people, and I’d never really made an environmental film. I mainly work as a filmmaker in African countries and I’d been interested for a while in telling a story about Congo that wasn’t the usual story of conflict and sexual violence. Those are obviously really important stories, but other narratives exist. Just like with “Skateistan,” I wanted to tell a hopeful story.
Q.
How did you learn about Virunga? Outside Africa there seems to be little awareness of the park.
A.
One day I picked up a paper in Sierra Leone, and there was a story about Andre caring for mountain gorillas, but it was really about Andre risking his life and why he had chosen to do that. So it was a story about rebirth in a part of the world where one only really heard negative, depressing stories. And that’s what initially interested me. When I got there, within a few days I learned about the oil problem. This was February 2012, and I realized there was a big investigative story that could potentially feed into everything else. And then this war started. So the story of hope and rebirth I initially tried to tell took this U-turn. But as a documentarian, you have to be flexible and allow the story to take you in different directions. I like to think the initial optimistic story is still there as a root throughout the film.
Q.
How do you make choices about all the story lines jostling for attention?
A.
I struggled. I’d been quite influenced by films like
“Dirty Wars
” and “The Cove,” which have a social issue at the heart of them, but they’d been created in a way that is much more dramatic. And I thought we might be able to do something similar. I thought the way to do that was to bring all the different elements I was filming — there’s this kind of nature documentary, this undercover investigation, and a sort of war movie as well — and a lot of people were telling me that was impossible. But I always felt that the key to really engaging audiences was to put them together. Because within those elements you have these really interesting cinematic positions between hope and the best of humanity and greed and the worst of humanity.
Q.
Their behavior sometimes seems almost human, but was it particularly difficult working with the gorillas?
A.
There were little moments when they destroyed a lot of equipment, so there would be little frustrations with them where I would be in the enclosure, and they would just tear my microphone off my camera. Within seconds they’d literally torn it to pieces. Or they would smudge muck all over the lens. But there also were funny things. I’d film with Andre not just because I needed the footage of him, but also because I found it a real relief from a scary situation. Because we’d hear bombs, over this four-month period, getting closer and closer every day. It was very tense, and we would be there and suddenly a gorilla would just let go with the loudest fart, and that’s amazing how that kills the tension. [Laughs]
Q.
In documentary films, directors often struggle with a balance between journalism and art. Your subject matter is inherently journalistic, and you’re also doing some investigative reporting. How did you strike that balance?
A.
We were quite constricted. We have to portray this thing 100 percent correctly from a journalistic point of view, because this is a billion-dollar company, and if we got anything wrong, they would have sued us. We had to play it quite straight with the journalism. And that was difficult because normally you have a voiceover that explains it all quite clearly. But artistically, I didn’t want a voiceover.
Q.
Why not? Were you looking for a verite kind of thing?
A.
I wanted the characters to speak for themselves. I wanted it to be their story. And whose voiceover would it be? I just felt it would be really odd. That would really have brought it back into documentary territory, and I wanted to push it a bit more into drama territory.
Q.
So how do you do that?
A.
Just in the way we edited it, interweaving these different story elements, character lines and themes, and in the end just bringing them all together. And I suppose some of the stuff with the way the park is  this living and breathing entity. We cut that against the more ugly human side of stuff.
Q.
How does it feel to be campaigning for an Oscar after enduring such tough conditions to make this film? Are you experiencing any kind of disconnect?
A.
It feels a long way from spending time in a tent in Congo. This was always about more than the film itself. To be included in this final 15 has brought a lot more visibility to the issues at its heart. If we were to be nominated, that would also massively bring an even brighter spotlight onto Virunga and the issues, and that is something that is fantastic.
Right now, with all that’s happened, it could all end tomorrow and I’d be incredibly humbled and proud. But I think the rangers expect a victory. When they were beginning to understand what I was doing, they would say, “So you’re going to win an Oscar for Virunga?” So there’s the real pressure, from a couple of hundred rangers and a couple of gorillas as well. [Laughs]

BATON ROUGE, La. —  David Duke seems a figure from the past, the former Klansman and white supremacist who two decades ago was almost elected Louisiana governor.
But this week when Representative Steve Scalise, the third-ranking House Republican leader, found himself trying to explain why he accepted a speaking engagement offered by a key aide to Mr. Duke in 2002, it was a reminder of the awkward dance and hard choices that Republicans in Louisiana faced in the 1990s when Mr. Duke was one of the most charismatic politicians in the state.
In his 1991 campaign for governor against Edwin W. Edwards, Mr. Duke largely avoided explicitly racial campaigning, appealed to the frustrations and resentments of white voters and won more than 60 percent of the white vote while losing in a runoff election. Two decades later, much of his campaign has merged with the political mainstream here, and rather than a bad memory from the past, Mr. Duke remains a window into some of the murkier currents in the state’s politics where Republicans have sought and eventually won Mr. Duke’s voters, while turning their back on him.
Echoing what mainstream Republicans did during the 1991 race for governor and since then, Mr. Scalise quickly distanced himself from Mr. Duke. Mr. Scalise said he only vaguely recalled his speech, had no forewarning it was a white nationalist group and would have avoided the meeting had he known.
Still, Roy Fletcher, a Baton Rouge-based political consultant who has managed campaigns for Republicans like former Gov. Mike Foster and Senator John McCain, said Mr. Duke may have become a toxic political personality, but he foreshadowed the state’s coming political and ideological shift.
“Now he doesn’t matter anymore,” Mr. Fletcher said. “But politicians here have still co-opted part of his message without having the same baggage.”
Louisiana, like most of the South, has become solidly Republican in a way it was not then, and race remains a fluid issue. The current governor, Bobby Jindal, is a conservative Republican of Indian descent whom Mr. Scalise supported.
Continue reading the main story
Mr. Duke, 64, who now calls himself a “human rights activist,” continues to sell books, a newsletter, DVDs, art and apparel and to speak on racial and cultural issues. He regularly tells audiences he is not a white supremacist and “condemns any form of racial supremacism and oppression.” But he rails against “the ultimate racists, the Jewish, Zionist tribalists.”
During the 1991 race for governor, Mr. Duke attempted to build a bridge between the Klansman he was and the polished politician he wanted to be. He told voters he regretted being “too intolerant” in his youth and said he would not disown his daughters if they brought home an African-American or Jewish boyfriend.
Instead, he focused on anti-big government and anti-tax mantras that preceded the
Tea Party movement
. His decision to run to the right of the field is now a common maneuver in Louisiana’s open primary system.
Continue reading the main story
Mr. Duke supported forcing welfare recipients to take birth control. Now there are near-perennial attempts by members of the Louisiana Legislature to give welfare recipients drug tests.
After being elected to the state House of Representatives in 1989, Mr. Duke filed nine bills, including measures implementing stricter guidelines for residents of public housing, repealing affirmative action programs and eliminating minority set-asides.
Stephanie Grace, a Louisiana political reporter and columnist for the past 20 years, first with The Times-Picayune in New Orleans and now The Advocate of Baton Rouge, recalled her first meeting with Mr. Scalise.
“He was explaining his politics and we were in this getting-to-know-each-other stage,” Ms. Grace said. “He told me he was like David Duke without the baggage. I think he meant he supported the same policy ideas as David Duke, but he wasn’t David Duke, that he didn’t have the same feelings about certain people as David Duke did.”
Mr. Scalise, his Washington staff and political consultant did not respond to emails, texts and phone calls over the past two days. Mr. Duke did not respond to an email sent through his website.
But Chuck Kleckley, the Republican speaker of the Louisiana House of Representatives, said Mr. Scalise’s conservative values should not be confused with Mr. Duke’s personal statements and actions. “It’s not fair to Steve at all,” Mr. Kleckley said. “He’s a good man, a good father, a good husband and a great person. Ever since I’ve known Steve, he wanted to do what’s right for Louisiana. I never felt like there was any kind of David Duke leanings with Steve.”
Jason Doré, the executive director of the Louisiana Republican Party, said Mr. Duke put it in the awkward position of campaigning for Mr. Edwards, who was later indicted on federal racketeering charges. The slogan, “Vote For the Crook: It’s Important,” caught on like wildfire in 1991. But he rejected the notion that Mr. Duke was somehow the architect of the state’s modern conservative politics.
“A lot of these things the conservative movement had supported, like limited government and a stronger defense, since Barry Goldwater and William F. Buckley,” Mr. Doré said. “We already supported a safety net over an entitlement mentality. David Duke did not invent this. He probably co-opted it.”
But if Mr. Duke became a third rail for Louisiana Republicans, some Republicans have seen value in courting Mr. Duke’s voters. When he successfully ran for Louisiana governor in 1995, Mr. Foster paid $150,000 for a list of Mr. Duke’s supporters and received his endorsement during the campaign. Mr. Foster said he never used the list, but it did result in a grand jury investigation and an ethics fine for the former governor after the expenditure was not properly reported.
And despite Mr. Scalise’s own statement on his speech to Mr. Duke’s European Unity and Rights Organization in 2002, its circumstances remain unclear.
Continue reading the main story
Continue reading the main story
Kenny Knight, an organizer for the group and a close associate of Mr. Duke’s, said that he invited Mr. Scalise to speak that day, but to a local group, not the full conference.
But Corey Ortis, who was a Louisiana representative for the organization from 2000 to 2004, said he attended the 2002 conference to hear from leaders of their movement, not Mr. Scalise. Still, from what he recalls of the event, Mr. Scalise gave a 10-to-15-minute presentation that was “the typical mainstream Republican thing” and not “too far right.”
“He touched on how America was founded on Christian principles, Christian men who founded this country, and how it was believed it would go forward as a Christian nation and how we’re getting away from that,” Mr. Ortis said.
Louisiana political experts say the demography of the state’s electorate has played as much of a role, if not larger, as Mr. Duke’s policy ideas in turning Louisiana solidly Republican. Pollster and data analyst John M. Couvillon, the president of JMC Enterprises of Louisiana, said a polarization has taken place to create a black-majority Democratic Party and a solidly white Republican Party.
He said the recent open primary election between the incumbent Senator Mary Landrieu, a Democrat, and Congressman Bill Cassidy, a Republican who won the seat, is proof enough. Landrieu carried only 18 percent of the white vote and Cassidy captured just 5 percent of the black vote, Mr. Couvillon said.
In concert with the 225,000 white Democrats who have left the party over the past 10 years, he said it has become very difficult for Democrats to win statewide in Louisiana without significant white support.
Still, he said, Republicans cannot rely on being an all-white party. “That’s the politics of division, which David Duke was good at it,” Mr. Couvillon said, “but it would be a foolish strategy if Louisiana Republicans were to espouse those same principles David Duke did. That’s a legacy best left behind.”

With its candy-colored dollhouse sets, miniaturized funicular and post-Weimar-era grandeur, “
The Grand Budapest Hotel
” offered moviegoers one of the most visually sumptuous confections of 2014.
What cineastes might not know is that the production designer behind those (mostly) cheery sets, Adam Stockhausen, 38, created them just weeks after finishing another widely lauded project: “12 Years a Slave,” which earned him an Academy Award nomination.
“It was completely, completely different,” Mr. Stockhausen said, surely earning an entry in the annals of understatement.
“I was in New Orleans and it was just the hottest summer ever,” he continued, “and then I went to Germany and it was the coldest winter and there was snow on the ground.
Mr. Stockhausen was chatting with the Bagger at the Gramercy Park Hotel in the fall, just before returning to  Germany to work on a Steven Spielberg film, about which he could divulge little. (“It’s the untitled Cold War spy thriller, I think is how we refer to it.”)
The climatic difference between Louisiana and Germany was just part of the adjustment for Mr. Stockhausen, who had spent much of 2012 painstakingly recreating antebellum estates and plantations in rural Louisiana, where much of “12 Years a Slave” was shot, in 100-plus degree heat. The work involved creating simulacrums of cotton plants by wiring hundreds of bolls to hibiscus stems – production predated Louisiana’s cotton season — and using reproductions of mid-19th-century shackles, which Mr. Stockhausen happened upon in a Mystic, Conn., blacksmith shop.
“It’s really heavy,” he said, of the emotional heft of using the shackles, “but finding that kind of stuff is really one of the special pleasures of this job.”
“The Grand Budapest Hotel” presented a whole different set of challenges, largely rooted in bringing the film director
Wes Anderson
’s whimsical visualizations to life.
While Mr. Stockhausen was still in New Orleans for “12 Years a Slave,” Mr. Anderson sent him little pen-and-ink drawings of how he wanted the
Grand Budapest Hotel itself
to look in relation to the town. But problematically, Mr. Stockhausen said, “that just doesn’t exist in reality or anywhere that we were looking to shoot.”
When Mr. Stockhausen and his team realized they wouldn’t be able to build a life-size hotel facade and funicular, they decided to combine paintings and miniatures. And when they set about producing a skiing sequence, they also knew that for multiple reasons – aesthetics, schedules, budgets – that they would not be shooting from a helicopter in the Alps. So they decided to try stop-motion, which ended up working charmingly.
“It was sweet and it all kind of came together,” Mr. Stockhausen said, “Knowing you want to go down the road, the path still kind of became more evident as we started doing it.”
One question burned in the Bagger’s mind throughout the chat: Given Mr. Stockhausen’s proven talents at design, surely he lives in a gemlike, cabinet-of-wonders apartment himself?
“No. Not at all. I wish. That would be lovely and I’m kind of working on that as a long-term plan, but no, unfortunately,” he said. “I have a very simple little garden apartment in Park Slope.”

Seven months after strutting the runway for Burberry during its Los Angeles fashion show, and five months after hosting the Council of Fashion Designers of America awards in New York,
James Corden
, the host of the “The Late Late Show,” is once again having a fashion moment: starring alongside Elton John and Naomi Campbell in the new Burberry holiday campaign directed by Christopher Bailey, the chief executive and chief creative officer of the brand. How did a portly British comedian become the latest “it” boy of the style set? In a phone call from Los Angeles, he talked through the story.
How did you end up in the new campaign?
Christopher asked me. I’ve known him for a few years now — I can’t remember if we met at the Met Ball, or maybe Anna Wintour’s house — and he’s always been very kind to me. When you look like me, there are not a mass of fashion houses rushing to dress you, you know, but he volunteered pretty early on.
Were you surprised?
I think the fact they asked me to do a runway thing in Los Angeles speaks volumes about
Burberry
. There they were, spending millions of dollars to launch this huge new store in L.A., and they decided to close their giant celebration with someone like myself. It’s really easy to look at fashion, or any other industry for that matter, and accuse them of taking themselves too seriously, but the thing about Christopher is that he takes his work very seriously, but not himself.
Were you at all concerned about the fact that the holiday campaign celebrates “Billy Elliot,” and there is something of a disjunction between what the film and show stand for — a way out of a very depressed working-class town — and the fact it is being used to sell high-end fashion?
That never occurred to me. I went to about as regular a comprehensive school as you could find in Buckinghamshire, and took every drama and dance class there was. I think the message of the film resonated with me, coming from where I come from, and Christopher coming from where he comes from, which is Yorkshire. It’s about aspiration, isn’t it: about the difference between not doing something and doing something? And doing something is what Christopher did.
What he did got him the top job at Burberry. We know he’s a successful creative director, but was he also a good short-film director?
I think if he wanted to direct a feature movie, he’d be great. If he wanted to be a furniture designer, he’d be great. I think he could probably win gold at the next Olympics in show jumping.
Do you like fashion?
I think fashion is a self-esteem industry. I always feel better when I put a great jacket on. I’ve never really been too cutting or acerbic about fashion.
What is it with comedians and fashion anyway? Before you, the CFDA was hosted by Seth Meyers and John Waters.
There’s a strange Venn diagram in this world, with fashion and comedy on very, very different sides. But where they meet is in showing off. Comedians love to show off, and fashion is all about showing off.

Lawyers from FanDuel and DraftKings appeared in New York State Supreme Court on Wednesday to fight efforts by the New York State attorney general,
Eric T. Schneiderman
, to bar state residents from playing daily fantasy sports contests on the companies’ websites.
The attorney general has argued that the games are based on chance and not on skill, an important distinction. Fantasy sports companies contend that their games are not gambling because they involve more skill than luck and were legally sanctioned by a 2006 federal law that exempted fantasy sports from a prohibition against processing online financial wagering.
On Wednesday, Judge Manuel Mendez said that he would make a ruling soon. Court observers took that to mean one or two weeks.
Mr. Schneiderman’s lawyers offered a range of arguments as to why the sites should be shut down in New York. A primary one, they said, was because winning the contests depends on a future event outside the players’ control.
Kathleen McGee, attorney for the state, argued that daily fantasy sports was clearly gambling because it depended on the outcome of events out of bettors’ control: a fumble, a batting slump, a dropped ball, injury and rain.
“I place my bet, pick my team and watch television,” she said. “Chance pervades daily fantasy sports.”
John Kiernan, representing FanDuel, argued that daily fantasy sports was not gambling at all.
“What is skill?” he said. “It’s when through effort and aptitude you increase your probabilities of success.”

The graduate student at the center of a scandal over a newly retracted
study
that has shaken trust in the conduct of social science apologized for lying about aspects of the study, including who paid for it and its methodology, but he said Friday in his first interview since the scandal broke that he stands by its finding that gay canvassers can influence voters’ attitudes on
same-sex marriage
.
The student, Michael J. LaCour, a doctoral candidate in political science at the University of California, Los Angeles, said the attack on his study — which was
retracted Thursday by the journal Science
— amounted to an academic ambush. “It’s completely unprecedented in the way it was done,” he said, referring to an account of the case posted by two colleagues last week, questioning his work. “They never contacted me directly, there was no transparency, and as a grad student I don’t have the same protection as a professor.”
Mr. LaCour disputes one of the main charges against him: that he improperly erased his raw data. That was one of the charges that led his co-author, Donald P. Green, a widely respected political scientist at Columbia University, to
ask the journal to retract the study
last week. The destruction of the data was not improper, he said, but in fact was required by U.C.L.A.’s institutional guidelines to protect study participants.
“At the end of the day, I was the one responsible for the raw data, and if something were to happen and reporters tracked people down, that’s a lawsuit,” he said.
But a researcher familiar with U.C.L.A. guidelines, but who declined to be identified by name because of the continuing investigation of the case at the university, said the language in the guidelines requires only that researchers erase “unique identifiers” and not the entire data set.
Mr. LaCour said he lied about the funding of his study to give it more credibility. He said that some of his colleagues had doubted his work because they thought he did not have enough money to pay for a such a complex study, among them David Broockman, a political scientist at Stanford and one of the authors of a
critique of his work
published last week. Mr. LaCour said he thought the funding sources he claimed would shore up the plausibility of the work. “I messed up in that sense, and it could be my downfall,” he said.
Three funding sources that Mr. LaCour listed as providing support for his published paper denied on Thursday that they had done so. The Ford Foundation, the Evelyn and Walter Haas Jr. Fund and the Williams Institute at U.C.L.A. said they had not given Mr. LaCour any money. But the Haas Jr. Fund had provided money to the group that Mr. LaCour was working with, the Los Angeles LGBT Center, and the graduate student had applied for and received a grant from the Williams Institute, but it came too late to help with the study, he said.
“The Ford Foundation grant did not exist,” Mr. LaCour wrote in
a public timelin
e posted late on Friday.

One of the most damning facts in the critical review of Mr. LaCour’s work was that the survey company he told the Los Angeles LGBT Center he was working with did not have any knowledge of his project. He now says that, in fact, he did not end up using that survey company but another one.
In an earlier interview, Dr. Green of Columbia said he had asked Mr. LaCour repeatedly to store his raw data in a databank at the University of Michigan. WASHINGTON —  In Tennessee, the state insurance commissioner approved a 36 percent rate increase for the largest health insurer in the state’s individual marketplace. In Iowa, the commissioner approved rate increases averaging 29 percent for the state’s dominant insurer.
Health insurance
consumers logging into
HealthCare.gov
on Sunday for the first day of the Affordable Care Act’s third open enrollment season may be in for sticker shock, unless they are willing to shop around. Federal officials acknowledged on Friday that many people would need to pick new plans to avoid substantial increases in premiums.
But, they said, even with a number of companies leaving the marketplace for health insurance under President Obama’s signature
health care law
, most people around the country will still be able to choose from three or more insurers in 2016.
“Shopping can save you money,” said Richard G. Frank, an assistant secretary of health and human services, who unveiled a huge collection of data on health plans that will go on sale on Sunday in the 38 states served by
HealthCare.gov
.
Consumers have until Jan. 31 to sign up, but must do so by Dec. 15 to obtain coverage starting on Jan. 1.
Mr. Frank, on leave from his position as a professor of health economics at Harvard, described the data in a positive light. “The Affordable Care Act has created a dynamic, competitive marketplace, with considerable choice and affordable premiums in 2016,” he said.
Consumers are not so sure.
“It really shocks me to see these plans with $5,000 deductibles,” Belinda Greb, 56, of Vida, Ore., said in an interview. “It becomes an area of stress as opposed to making me feel secure.”
Federal subsidies for low- and moderate-income consumers will keep pace with premiums for a benchmark plan, the second-lowest-cost “silver” plan, Mr. Frank said, and consumers who choose that plan can protect themselves and their wallets.
“The vast majority of marketplace consumers receive tax credits that insulate them from premium increases,” Mr. Frank said.
A typical family of four with annual income of $60,000 will, on average, receive tax credits totaling $5,570 in 2016, up from $4,850 this year, the administration said.
But some consumers who have recently received renewal notices have been shocked by the decisions they face.
Ms. Greb said she was too upset to finish a letter she got recently from her insurer, Moda Health, that said her “bronze” health plan, for which she pays $213 a month after a subsidy of $175, would not be offered through the exchange in 2016. The company offered her a similar plan that would cost $265 a month if her subsidy stays the same.
The new plan recommended by Moda has a deductible, the amount she must pay for care before the insurance begins to pay, of $5,500, up from $4,250 in her current plan, she said. “People are putting off care because of the expense.”
The Obama administration said nearly nine out of 10 consumers with marketplace coverage would be able to choose from three or more insurers in 2016. That is important, Mr. Frank said, because in insurance and other industries, “competition intensifies when there are three or more firms in a market.”

TAMPA, Fla. —  At a downtown park here on April 26, the Sexual Violence Task Force of Tampa Bay will host a “Take Back the Night” rally, a candlelight vigil and silent march to raise sexual assault awareness.
Four days later, and less than five miles away, executives sitting in the Tampa Bay Buccaneers’ gleaming office complex must decide whether to use the first pick of the N.F.L. draft on Jameis Winston, the Florida State quarterback who was accused of raping a fellow student in 2012. Winston, 21, has asserted his innocence, did not face criminal charges and was recently cleared by Florida State of violating the university’s student code of conduct.
The downtrodden Buccaneers need a quarterback, and Winston, a Heisman Trophy winner in 2013, is seen as one of the top two available. But Winston’s checkered past — he was also involved in BB gun incidents, cited for shoplifting and suspended one game for shouting an obscene phrase on campus — has presented the team, and its fans, with a quandary that has divided and unsettled the Tampa Bay community.
In the wake of last year’s graphic video that showed the former Baltimore Ravens running back Ray Rice punching his future wife and the firestorm the league’s initial, light punishment of Rice generated, the N.F.L. announced that it was taking domestic violence and sexual assault matters more seriously. With the league’s general reputation in mind, however, it is unclear if the N.F.L. has substantively changed any policies when it comes to vetting draft prospects in the aftermath of the Rice scandal.
The Buccaneers are not commenting on how they plan to use their prized first pick. A team spokesman said they were evaluating all the draft prospects and would not speak publicly about any specific player.
Representatives of the sexual violence task force, however, have visited with members of the Tampa Bay front office. Asked about the prospect of the Bucs selecting Winston, the task force’s chairwoman, Amanda Brennan, said in a statement: “The larger issue is that there have been many allegations against Jameis Winston, yet there is no question that Jameis Winston will be chosen by an N.F.L. team to play next season. As an N.F.L. player, he is a role model for boys and young men across the country. The Sexual Violence Task Force of Tampa Bay would like to know that Jameis Winston will be expected to adhere to a strict standard of conduct.”
Continue reading the main story
Predicting how Winston will behave off the field as a highly paid professional football player has become the consuming focus of as many as 20 N.F.L. teams, who have begun exhaustive examinations into Winston’s past.
“He’s brought the scrutiny on himself, and how he deals with the next three or four months will be a big part of every team’s evaluation.” said Mike Mayock, a former N.F.L. player who is now a top draft analyst for the NFL Network.
Compiling a comprehensive report on Winston’s background will be crucial because several draft experts have predicted that Winston, despite his troubles, will be a top-five pick, or maybe even the first overall selection.
Continue reading the main story
“He’s had off-the-field issues, but if he checks out and you can reconcile that all of that is behind him and not going to happen again,” ESPN’s Mel Kiper Jr., a draft analyst, said, “then he goes No. 1.”
With all that at stake, teams will employ every resource at their disposal — scouts, coaches, executives, psychologists, orthopedists, private detectives, criminal investigators, security agents, cognitive test specialists and personality assessment clinicians — to gather information on Winston.
The N.F.L. combine, a multiple-day skills audition, is in mid-February. Winston will train with a quarterback guru, but he will also be schooled for the dozens of interviews he will have with team executives.
“His agents will get him to a professional interview coach who will instruct him how to dress, act, sit and talk to the teams,” said Brian Billick, who won a Super Bowl as coach of the Baltimore Ravens and is now an NFL Network commentator. “He’ll learn some mantra about learning from his mistakes or how he has matured and is ready for the next step.”
Behind the scenes, Winston’s behavioral patterns, personality and temperament will be examined. Teams will ask Winston to take a Wonderlic test, a cognitive ability exam that dates to the 1930s. But without Winston’s approval or participation, the N.F.L., as well as individual teams, will scour through the minute details of Winston’s life.
“Everyone in the team’s organizational chart makes some calls to their counterparts around the country,” Mayock said. “The equipment guys might call the equipment guys at Florida State, and the public-relations guy calls around to the college sports information directors he knows who might have dealt with Winston.”
Other team employees will be sent to Winston’s hometown in Alabama to interview high school or grade-school teachers, coaches, classmates and friends. Most teams go straight to professional detectives, some of whom are former F.B.I. agents or retired police officers.
For many years, the Giants used a former insurance fraud investigator who was a licensed detective and had ties to local, regional and federal law enforcement officials. The investigator created a file of stories, interview transcripts, depositions and court cases about whatever prospect was being considered. He met with the Giants’ brain trust away from the team’s complex so the information could be shared with only select officials.
Separately, the N.F.L., which employs more than 70 independent investigators, does background checks on each of the 360 players invited to the combine and scours social media for clues to their character or to potential problems. The N.F.L. also has a remittance policy in which teams must pay fines if too many of their players have off-the-field issues. The reports on the 360 players are hand-delivered to the 32 teams.
In the wake of the Rice scandal, the N.F.L. appointed four women to executive positions and said they would influence the league’s policies in the future. Anna Isaacson, the vice president for community affairs and philanthropy, was given an expanded role as vice president of social responsibility. The league also retained Lisa Friel, the former head of the sex crimes prosecution unit in the Manhattan district attorney’s office, as a senior adviser. (The league would not make any of them available for interviews.)
Continue reading the main story
Continue reading the main story
But even the existing level of scrutiny raises hundreds of red flags in the pool of draft picks.
“I have said that young and stupid should be one word,” Billick said. “But it’s not always serious, and what you’re really looking for is a pattern. Was it a mistake that showed immaturity, or is it a recurring thing and an indication of his true personality and his way of doing things?
“That’s what might hurt Winston the most — his pattern of behavior.”
Winston is not the first high-profile prospect to enter the N.F.L. under a cloud of suspicion. The draft statuses of several players, including Johnny Rodgers in the 1970s, Charles White in the 1980s, Lawrence Phillips in the 1990s and Aaron Hernandez in 2010, were adversely affected by prominent off-field concerns.
But it is also true that each was drafted and played in the N.F.L. Some managed to avoid more serious trouble. Phillips and Hernandez are now behind bars.
As investigations and evaluations of Winston are completed this spring, some teams will pass on Winston. But other teams will hope Winston falls from a first-round pick to a second- or third-round selection. It is a curious moral judgment.
“It is money, pure and simple,” Mayock said. “It is less of an economic risk in the third round because it costs less to sign that player.”
For the teams that still value Winston as a first-round pick, the decision is likely to be made at a team’s highest levels.
“Only an idiot would fail to recognize the heightened sense of concern about these kinds of offenses right now,” Billick said. “And for a change, you might see several owners get very active in the draft process for that reason. Although it won’t prevent someone from taking Jameis Winston.”

To the Editor:
Re “
60 Million People Fleeing Chaotic Lands, U.N. Says
” (front page, June 18):
The number of refugees sounds overwhelming. The response from the United States and the developed world, however, is underwhelming.
The number of displaced people fleeing persecution is more than twice what it was in 2005, and higher than at any time since the Holocaust and the end of World War II. Yet this year’s refugee resettlement ceiling is the same as 10 years ago: 70,000. Last year, each of us contributed only $4.39 in taxpayer money to help refugees overseas.
The American experience tells us that refugees who are welcomed and allowed to work, whether here or in their country of first asylum, are an asset to society. When marginalized or warehoused in camps, they are a burden.
As we commemorate World Refugee Day on June 20, our government should commit to contributing much more to welcoming and helping refugees rebuild their lives.
MARK HETFIELD
New York
The writer is president and chief executive of HIAS, a global Jewish nonprofit that protects refugees.

Over seven seasons, the character Peggy Olson on “Mad Men” grew from mousy secretary to advertising dynamo. While that AMC show may have started out focusing on the man in the corner office, in the end it was Peggy’s journey that captivated and compelled many viewers. While Don Draper battled inner demons, Peggy battled society, pushing the boundaries of what women could achieve in the work force of the 1960s.
Having earned a sixth Emmy nomination for the role,
Elisabeth Moss
has to figure out how to follow it. “Before ‘Mad Men,’ ” she said, “I was unemployed a lot, and so I’m still so happy anytime anyone offers me a role. Now I am learning to get over that first instinct and to make sure I am doing things that are really thought out.”
These are edited excerpts from a conversation in which Ms. Moss spoke about “Mad Men,” her latest Emmy nomination, and whether there will be a second season of Jane Campion’s “Top of the Lake.”
Q.
When “Mad Men” ended, were you immediately bombarded with requests? How did you pick what to do next?
A.
I had already signed up for “High Rise,” the Ben Wheatley film, before we wrapped, so I left to do that right away. And then I did, like, three more films after that. I don’t really have a conscious plan; I just want to do great material. I suppose there is definitely a part of me that is more interested in doing films because of the time commitment, but that’s just for right now, and that could change tomorrow if I found something that I couldn’t turn down.
Q.
After being on a series for so long, the variety must be nice.
A.
Yes, exactly. As an actor, it’s awesome to play, like, three different characters in one year, as opposed to the same for so many. Although, you know, woe is me, having to play Peggy for so many years. Poor me.
Q.
There were some mixed feelings among viewers about Peggy’s ending — she got to be in love, but she didn’t leave to start a business with Joan.
A.
If she had gone off with Joan, she wouldn’t have been a writer. She would have been making commercials; it would not have actually been what she loved. I felt kind of the same way at first, like, oh my God, Joan and Peggy! You want them to move in together and become best friends and order pizza.
Her ending up with Stan — I loved it. I mean, why not? The thing is, you know she’s going to have career success. You know she’s going to end up running a company. That’s not a surprise. What you don’t know is if she finds personal happiness and finds love. So I think the fact that we gave her that is so much more interesting. Because it’s actually the thing she struggled with for so many years. And I also think, as a feminist, you don’t have to not have love to have success in your career. To me, it’s actually a very kind of feminist moment where she’s saying, ‘Yes, I’m going to have my cake and eat it, too.’ ”
Q.
Speaking of feminism, do you think Peggy would have gotten really involved in the bra-burning feminist movement of the ’70s?

No, not at all. We know her path, because it happened. We know what happened to those women; they exist in real life. CHICAGO —  For decades, they had waited for an apology. This group of black men, some now graying and bent by age, had complained of violent abuse at the hands of the police in the 1970s and ’80s on this city’s South Side. They said they had been suffocated with plastic bags, beaten with phone books, shocked with cattle prods — torture tactics meant to extract confessions to crimes.
On Wednesday, after years of investigation, public debate and litigation, the City of Chicago expressed remorse. City Council members voted without dissent to pay $5.5 million in reparations to victims of torture and abuse by a group of officers known as the “Midnight Crew” and overseen by a notorious police commander, Jon Burge.
For those affected, there were also promises of a memorial, psychological counseling and job training, and assurances that their story would be taught in Chicago schools.
“This is another step, but an essential step, in righting a wrong, removing a stain on the reputation of this great city and the people who make up this great city,” Mayor Rahm Emanuel said.
For the victims, like Anthony Holmes, who spent 30 years in prison for a 1973 murder he says he falsely confessed to after being tortured, it meant the prospect of relief.
“I don’t care how you try to forget it, how you try to put it to the side,” Mr. Holmes said. “It’s always there and at times it comes out on you. You might break down and start crying.”
As a broad conversation about police conduct and race plays out in cities like Baltimore and Ferguson, Mo., Chicagoans, too, are re-examining relations with the police, including episodes more recent than those tied to Mr. Burge.
On Wednesday, the City Council approved a $415,000 settlement with a woman who said she had been sexually assaulted in 2011 by two on-duty police officers, who have since resigned and pleaded guilty to criminal charges of official misconduct. Protesters have objected to a decision last month by a judge to drop charges against an off-duty Chicago police officer who shot and killed an unarmed black woman, Rekia Boyd, in 2012. And many say they are awaiting the fate of a police officer who shot and killed Laquan McDonald, who was 17 and carrying a knife when he was shot 16 times last fall.
Over the past decade, the City of Chicago has spent more than $500 million on settlements, judgments, fees and other costs related to police misconduct,
according to a 2014 investigation
by the Better Government Association, a nonpartisan watchdog group. Andy Shaw, who leads the association, said the city could have used the money to hire more police officers or teachers, or to balance the city’s troubled budget.
More than 20 years after Mr. Burge was fired from the Chicago Police Department, some people in the city’s toughest neighborhoods say that dealings with the police have grown tense, particularly in the last few years as city officials worked to tamp down a
high homicide rate
linked to a pervasive gang problem.

“I don’t see the times being better at all,” said Mark Clements, 50, a torture victim whose name was read at the Council meeting on Wednesday. “I see these times more so as being times of near-riot.”
Late last month, Garry McCarthy, the city’s police superintendent, announced plans for a tour around the city aimed at building trust between police and residents. And police officials say they have worked to make other improvements, too: expanding bike and foot patrols in neighborhoods, creating community policing offices in all police districts, and launching a pilot program for body cameras.
In a statement, the Chicago Police Department said: “Jon Burge’s actions are a disgrace — to Chicago, to the hard-working men and women of the police department, and most importantly to those he was sworn to protect. Mayor Emanuel and Superintendent McCarthy have zero tolerance for any misconduct.”
The cases related to Mr. Burge and the officers under his command had plagued this city for decades. In 2010, special prosecutors issued a report corroborating the abuse claims. By then, though, statutes of limitation on abuse charges had run out. Instead, Mr. Burge was convicted in 2010 of perjury and obstruction of justice; he completed his prison sentence this year.
Reached by phone at his home in Florida, Mr. Burge declined to comment on the reparations.

New York City is looking to join Chicago, Houston, Denver and other major cities by passing legislation to create its first comprehensive cultural plan.
The legislation, which the City Council passed by a vote of 49 to 0 on Tuesday,  requires the city to analyze its current cultural priorities, assess how service to different neighborhoods can be improved, study the condition of arts organizations and artists, and plan how the city can remain artist-friendly in a time of high rents and other economic pressures.
The bill was introduced by the council members Stephen Levin (Brooklyn) and
Jimmy Van Bramer
(Queens).
“Administrations come and go; cultural affairs commissioners come and go,” said Mr. Van Bramer, who is chairman of the council’s cultural affairs committee and majority leader. “What we want is to have this ongoing prioritization of arts and culture.”
Tom Finkelpearl, the city’s cultural affairs commissioner, said he fully supported the plan. “We went back and forth and back and forth on improving the bill and I have completely come around to the idea that it’s going to be great for New York,” he said.
“Even though I spend all my time out looking at everything in all the boroughs, it still only adds up to an anecdotal idea of what’s happening,” he continued. “Are there parts of the city that are not adequately served by cultural resources or are there imaginative ideas for getting cultural resources to those communities?”
The plan requires the city to find out what arts groups in the five boroughs want and need and to incorporate these recommendations in a plan to be submitted by July 1, 2017.
“Up to this point, we haven’t had a clearly articulated vision for culture in this city,” Mr. Levin said, “a written document we can point to that says, ‘This is how we’re doing things.’”
The bill was first introduced in 2013.
Denver’s cultural plan — “Imagine 2020,” announced last year — established 50 goals for developing arts in the city, while also identifying obstacles to those targets. New York’s plan will study arts education, incorporate culture into community and economic development, and seek the cooperation of other city agencies.
To review the plan and advise the
Cultural Affairs Department
, a citizens advisory committee will be appointed by the mayor, the speaker and the borough presidents.
“Some folks have clearly said we could do better in reaching deeper into neighborhoods that are underserved by the arts,” Mr. Van Bramer said. “I would agree.”

The charter school movement got its foothold two decades ago by promising that independently operated schools would outperform their traditional counterparts if they were allowed to receive public money while being exempted from some state regulations — including the requirement that they be unionized. Charter advocates made the deal more compelling by vowing that charter schools would be closely overseen and shut down when they failed , in contrast to traditional schools, which were allowed to fail in perpetuity without consequence.
The system has worked reasonable well in New York City, where data show that the typical charter school student learns more in reading and math in a year that his or her traditional school peers, giving ammunition to anti-union critics who say that union contracts strip schools of the flexibility in hiring, firing and general management that they need to run well.
New York City’s union, The United Federation of Teachers, set out to disprove that theory in 2005, when it opened its own charter school in the East New York section of Brooklyn. Randi Weingarten, who led the U.F.T. at the time – and who now leads the American Federation of Teachers – upped the ante by
predicting that
the school would “show real, quantifiable student achievement and with those results, finally dispel the misguided and simplistic notion that the union contract is an impediment to success.”
That’s not how things have worked out. The school struggled almost from the start. The State University of New York came close to revoking its charter in 2013 – and probably should have done so. This past year, just 11 percent of its third-through eighth-grade students scored as proficient or better on the state reading tests, compared with 29 percent in the city as a whole.
The union admitted defeat last week,
saying that it would close
the kindergarten-through-eighth-grade portion of the school because of low test scores. The current U.F. T. president, Richard Mulgrew, blamed state test score requirements for the school’s problems.
But the record shows that the union failed the children in this school at just about every level. When the school’s charter came up for renewal in 2013, the SUNY panel cited all kinds of problems including: excessive principal turnover; poor instructional skills and teacher coaching; and deficiencies in the way the school handled English language learners and special education students.
What’s striking is that the school was managed poorly even after the union staked its reputation on the project. This suggests that the union either did not take the charter project seriously – or that it knows less about running schools than it thinks.

Asked about her upbringing in a Union City, N.J., household in which her father, Robert Menendez, was a New Jersey assemblyman and her mother was working in the state’s public schools, Alicia Menendez said: “I grew up driven and nerdy and feeling a sense of responsibility to help people. My mother was a go-getter and guidance counselor, and Dad was an original tiger mom who expected nothing short of excellence.”
A case in point: When she was in second grade, Ms. Menendez agonized over possibly staying home from school to nurse a cold, and when she took the day off, her father, a Democrat who is now the senior United States senator from New Jersey, wanted to know why she didn’t have perfect attendance.
By third grade, she wrote a school report about Gloria Steinem, which served her well when she later attended Harvard, earning a bachelor’s degree in women, gender and sexuality. She followed that up by working in various capacities to increase political participation among women, minorities and young Americans.
But it was while writing a freelance article in December 2008, about the growing influence of Hispanic voters that she happened upon a bright young man named Carlos Prío Odio, who had been the deputy Latino vote director on the 2008 Obama presidential campaign.
She tracked down Mr. Odio expecting to engage him in a stimulating conversation that would produce an informative article, but the interview fell flat when Mr. Odio refused to answer most of her questions.
“I thought she was pushy,” he said. “I was waiting for a job in the Obama administration and didn’t want to say anything that would get me in trouble. She got irritated, and that irritated me.”
“We definitely rubbed each other the wrong way,” said Ms. Menendez, now 31 and the host of “Alicia Menendez Tonight,” a cultural affairs talk show on Fusion, an ABC-Univision joint television venture in Miami.
For the next few months, they ran in the same political circles, but without actually bumping into each other. “I rolled my eyes when I heard her name mentioned,” said Mr. Odio, 32 and a graduate of American University.
“We talked trash about each other,” Ms. Menendez said.
Then Mr. Odio’s close friend and colleague, Stephanie Valencia-Ramirez, unaware of their history, decided to forge a connection between Mr. Odio and Ms. Menendez at a reception in September 2009 at the National Museum of American History. “Alicia and Carlos are the next generation Cuban royalty, so I introduced them,” said Mrs. Valencia-Ramirez, now the deputy chief of staff at the Commerce Department in Washington.
Although Ms. Menendez had a boyfriend at the time, sparks flew immediately.
“I turned around and saw this stunning creation,” recalled Mr. Odio, who was born and raised in Miami watching “The West Wing,” and had by then become the deputy associate director in the White House Office of Political Affairs. “She looked even better than in her YouTube clips where she was often angry and yelling. So I said, ‘Alicia Menendez.’ And she responded, ‘Carlos Odio.’ Then we hugged. It was an instant truce!”
Continue reading the main story
At that moment, she understood why she had thought he was so full of himself. “On the phone he’d been aloof, but in person, he was intense and charming,” said Ms. Menendez, who was then the communications director in Washington for Democracia U.S.A., a Latino voter registration and engagement group. As the night unfolded, Emilio Estefan Jr., the Cuban-American musician and producer, and husband of Gloria Estefan, invited them to join a group of people at a Greek-Mediterranean tapas restaurant in Washington, where Ms. Menendez and Mr. Odio were seated beside each other.
Eager to engage Ms. Menendez, Mr. Odio, who had recently ended a relationship, wisely played the “Cuban card,” doling out information that his mother, Marían Prío Odio, a retired psychotherapist, was the executive director of the Miami Mental Health Center, and that his father, Cesar H. Odio, had been the city manager of Miami from 1985 to 1996. Not only that, his maternal grandfather, Carlos Prío Socarrás, was the president of Cuba from 1948 to 1952.
They talked about Cuba, their own public service backgrounds, and how Mr. Odio had once done volunteer work for Senator Menendez. They learned each was a workaholic with no hobbies except reading.
“Carlos was
wow
!
” she said. “When he wanted to know about my women’s studies thesis, it was without the usual ‘I also studied women in college’ that often accompanies such questions.”
She concluded: “The bravado I’d perceived in our first conversation was just a front for someone who was actually much more complicated, much more generous. His brain worked like jazz, it was all over the place. He never let the ball drop. It was electric.”
But neither was looking for love, they say, especially after having been in various long-term relationships since their teenage years. In fact, Ms. Menendez was ready to be on her own for a while. After dinner, Mr. Odio put her in a cab and then joined friends at a bar.
But she couldn’t get him out of her mind. “I went from harboring serious disdain for this person I thought I knew, to walking away from that dinner and thinking, ‘Oh, man, this could be it,’ ” she said.
About a month later, Ms. Menendez texted him that she was with her dad (who was divorced from her mother in 2005) and they had “nothing in the refrigerator” to eat. Despite feeling wiped out from his long hours in the White House, Mr. Odio read her loud and clear. He called to make a dinner date.
The next night, at a Washington restaurant, theirs was the sort of subdued conversation one might expect from two workaholics winding down at the end of a long day. Yet both were conscious that they were beginning a relationship.
Soon they were dining together nearly every night. “Alicia was endlessly fascinating, deeply complex,” he said. “I’d assumed things about her based on her schooling — Harvard, ugh — and in talking to her, I saw pretty quickly that she was both this wonder woman and one of the most self-aware and emphatic people I’d ever met.”
Continue reading the main story
“Alicia is smart and open, a bright light who all of the guys like,” said Kim Corbin, a longtime friend of Ms. Menendez. “But Carlos immediately saw more than that in her.”
In spring 2010, Ms. Menendez and Mr. Odio moved in together. Things went smoothly as they grew more comfortable with each other’s quirks. She is organized; he is not. She has a need for solitude and chill time after traveling for work; he takes pleasure in injecting humor into her life.
Continue reading the main story
“Alicia has always challenged Carlos and keeps him on his toes,” said his younger sister
Sarah Odio-Torlage
, now a policy aide to the Miami-Dade County Commissioner Xavier Suarez. “He was in awe of her from the very beginning.”
Still, frustration was bubbling up over his long hours in the White House. “I understood that,” Ms. Menendez said. “But I would make him elaborate meals then have to eat them alone.”
The late nights ended the following year, when Mr. Odio became director of the Candidate Project, a nonpartisan group that recruits progressives for local office, which allowed him to indulge in his passion for grassroots activism. Ms. Menendez, meanwhile, was eager to shed her policy work for a job in the news media.
She got her wish: An offer came to host and produce HuffPost Live, a web-based video streaming network that is a part of The Huffington Post. But it meant moving to New York, which was not where Mr. Odio needed to be.
Nevertheless, he supported her move. “Carlos wanted me to do this and was not intimidated,” she said. “He put me first and coached me. We were both young and still finding ourselves in work and life. We were hoping to move forward as a couple even though we would be living apart.”
When Ms. Menendez left for Manhattan, they made plans to see each other every other weekend — he from Miami where he had moved in with his mother and father (whose position as Miami’s city manager had
ended in a jail term
following a political corruption probe).
It was her job, this time, that demanded a serious investment of time. (She co-anchored five hours of breaking news coverage during the hunt for the Boston bomber and six hours of live coverage for 2012 election night.) They would rendezvous in either New York or Miami, but not often enough.
Their frustrations grew when their separations would go on for weeks, but Mr. Odio, who went out on his own as a consultant to those looking to provide funding for political causes, helped them develop a rhythm. “Carlos integrated himself into my life in New York without being there,” she said.
They had enjoyed the thrill of rushing into a dynamic relationship, the benefits of living together and the maturity of surviving apart. “This period of separation proved to me that they were really a strong couple,” Mr. Odio’s father said. “Alicia is a determined and intelligent human being, and Carlos respects her in every sense. They are lucky to have found each other.”
“Living in separate cities was great for our frequent-flier status, but not for the idea of marriage,” said Ms. Menendez, who moved to Miami in May 2013 for Mr. Odio and her current job at Fusion.
Continue reading the main story
Continue reading the main story
Ms. Menendez was ready for a ring, but as that long hot summer wound on, she began to worry that her boyfriend had developed “a Caribbean sense of time,” she said.
Mr. Odio, however, had bought her a ring even before she moved to Miami. He was waiting for the right moment (September 2013) to surprise her.
That day, Ms. Menendez was headed to Washington for a girlfriend’s birthday, so he cooked up a ruse about having to fly to a conference in Cleveland. Instead, he waved his goodbyes and then jumped on a different Washington-bound flight.
Once there, he surprised her at the National Museum of American History, the scene of their first face-to-face conversation.
“I was wandering around looking at exhibits,” she said. “When I turned a corner, there he was.” On one knee.
The couple wed on Feb. 15 at the Coral Gables United Church of Christ in Florida, where 162 of the couple’s family members and friends had gathered. Flanked by her parents, the bride walked down the aisle wearing a custom ivory Anne Barge gown with a sweeping chapel train.
The service, which was performed by the Rev. Dr. Guillermo Marquez-Sterling, emphasized the importance of community and family. It also celebrated how life can be better when two people help each other become all they dream to be.
After the couple kissed as husband and wife, the crowd cheered, then headed for the reception in
Comber Hall,
a part of the Church of the Little Flower, a few blocks away.
Between dances, friends acknowledged that much of the attraction between the bride and groom was on a different level of intellect, art and politics than either had experienced before.
“Alicia and Carlos are unconventional people who push the envelope in an effort to make the world better,” Mrs. Valencia-Ramirez said. “To be able to match that in each other surprised them both.”
“When I met Carlos, I wasn’t quite sure,” quipped Senator Menendez during his toast to the couple. “I thought he was a cocky guy, but then I realized that if he is going to hang with Alicia, he had better be smart and confident.”
The bride’s father went on to offer the couple advice that hasn’t quite taken hold in his Senate day job: “Love constantly, blame slowly, forgive quickly and be best friends.”

To the Editor:
Re “
Bring the Basket Down and Fandom Up
,” by Asher Price (Op-Ed, June 2), which suggests lowering the basket for the Women’s National Basketball Association:
I much prefer women’s basketball to the men’s game specifically because there is virtually no dunking in the women’s game. I find dunking in the men’s game to be one of the most selfish maneuvers in all of sports.
Instead of swaggering and swooping, the women’s game relies entirely on good fundamentals, good teamwork and good hustle. That is what I find exciting about team sports. I prefer baseball games in which there are no home runs but lots of smart play and good hustle for the same reason.
As for selling tickets, lowering the rim for the women might attract some new fans, but it might also alienate a lot of current fans.
SAM GREEN
Charlottesville, Va.
To the Editor:
I could not agree more with Asher Price’s article about lowering the basket so the women can dunk to excite the fans in the stands.
Title IX gives equal opportunity for women to play sports in schools, but does not say that they have to play by the same regulations as men. If college administrators would ask for such a small change, I suspect that the National Collegiate Athletic Association would agree. I bet that the fans would not even notice the change if they didn’t know about it. I watched many volleyball games at Fordham University but never knew that the women’s net was almost eight inches shorter than the men’s net.
I only wish that the Women’s World Cup, which starts on Saturday in Canada, would be played with a lighter ball (a half-size smaller, size 4.5) on a 100-yard-long field instead of 110 or 120 yards. The game would be much faster and more interesting, with lots of action in front of the keepers and probably lots of goals for fans to enjoy.
NESS SELMANI
Staten Island
The writer was the women’s soccer coach at Fordham University from 1996 to 2014.
To the Editor:
Like Asher Price, I look forward to more dunking of the ball in the W.N.B.A. But I want it to happen on the basis of ever-increasing athleticism, not on the basis of a lowered hoop.
Like Mr. Price, and many others who enjoy women’s basketball, I want to increase the attendance at W.N.B.A. games. I also support making W.N.B.A. rules more similar to those of the international sport.
Many factors, including marketing, are necessary to bring more fans to the league (although any sport played indoors during the summer will have a challenge attracting large numbers of attendees). But I doubt that one of the effective factors will be the lowering of the basket. I wouldn’t try to get more fans to watch track by shortening the 100 meters to a quicker 90.
One of the reasons that I like the W.N.B.A. is that it’s different from the great N.B.A. Even monster dunks can become routine. Does the N.B.A. want to freshen up its game? It could
raise
its baskets.
CARL WOIDECK
Eugene, Ore.
